# STS Second Brain

Start here. This is a map of content, not a container — every note below lives
in its own file and links onward.

## Reference library

- [[Reference library]] — catalogue of the standards, papers and texts held locally

## Standards

- [[AS 1726 soil and rock description]] — how we describe what comes out of the ground
- [[AS 2159 piling]] — what governs bored pier construction and acceptance
- [[AS 2870 residential site classification]] — reactive site classes

## Materials

- [[Soil description order]] — the sequence we write descriptions in
- [[Rock weathering classes]] — XW through FR, and what each means for founding
- [[Rock strength classes]] — EL through EH and the field tests behind them
- [[Weathered siltstone]] — the founding material on most Sydney basin jobs

## Methods

- [[Bored pier inspection]] — what to check and record at the base of a pier
- [[Rock socket length]] — how socket length is specified, measured and reported
- [[DCP testing]] — blow counts to allowable bearing pressure
- [[Reduced levels and datums]] — RL conventions and the mistakes that follow from getting them wrong
- [[Groundwater observations]] — what a water level in a hole does and does not tell you
- [[Borehole log conventions]] — how our logs are laid out and why

## Working with AI

- [[Reverse prompting]] — hand over context, let the agent ask what it is missing
- [[Graph engineering]] — dependency maps, the fake-edge test, diamonds and checkers

## Decisions

- [[Why pile data carries provenance]] — the Field state model in the pile viewer
- [[Socket compliance is indeterminate by default]] — why unknown never reads as pass

## Templates

- [[Template - site inspection note]]
- [[Template - decision]]

# Open in Obsidian

1. Open Obsidian → **Open folder as vault**
2. Choose the folder this file is in (`STS-Second-Brain`)
3. Trust the vault when prompted — the only thing in `.obsidian/` is graph and
   appearance settings, no plugins or scripts

Graph view is on the left ribbon, or `Ctrl+G`. It comes pre-coloured by folder:

| Colour | Folder |
|---|---|
| Violet | the index |
| Blue | standards |
| Green | materials |
| Orange | methods |
| Red | decisions |
| Amber | reference library |
| Grey | templates |

Local graph (`Ctrl+Shift+G` or the note's ⋮ menu) shows what one note connects
to, which is usually more useful than the whole graph once the vault grows.

## Keeping it in step with the web viewer

The Markdown here is the source of truth. After editing, regenerate the web
viewer's index from the repo:

```bash
node scripts/build-vault-index.mjs
```

The repo copy lives at `sts-playground/second-brain/`. If you edit here and
there, they will drift — pick one as the working copy.

## Related

- [[Index]]

notes.title: Socket compliance is indeterminate by default
notes.body:
# Socket compliance is indeterminate by default

**Decision.** When the required socket length is unknown, socket compliance
returns `indeterminate` — never `compliant`.

## Reasoning

Compliance is achieved measured against required. Our inspection reports carry
the achieved length; the requirement lives on the structural drawing, which we
often do not hold. A tool that defaults to pass in that situation manufactures an
engineering conclusion out of an absence of data.

`indeterminate` is a first-class answer with its own colour in the 3D scene,
deliberately not the same orange as a verified socket, so an unassessed pier
cannot read as approved at a glance.

## What it means in practice

On the Carter Street job all 18 inspected piers report as compliance-unknown,
because the report states no required socket. That is the correct reading of the
available information, and it makes the missing document visible.

## Related

- [[Rock socket length]]
- [[AS 2159 piling]]
- [[Why pile data carries provenance]]

notes.title: Why pile data carries provenance
notes.body:
# Why pile data carries provenance

**Decision.** Every engineering value in the pile viewer is a `Field<T>` carrying
value, state, source and confidence, rather than a bare number.

States: `extracted`, `calculated`, `manual`, `inferred`, `verified`,
`conflicting`, `missing`.

## The problem it solves

Once a number is in a spreadsheet it looks like every other number. A toe level
read off a signed report and a toe level someone estimated from a drawing render
identically, and by the time it matters nobody can tell which is which.

## Consequences

- A missing value stays missing all the way to the screen. A pile with no toe
  level has no length — it does not have a length of zero.
- When two sources disagree the field is `conflicting`, both values are kept, and
  the engineer resolves it. Source priority orders them for review; it does not
  pick a winner, because a higher-priority document is only better if it is also
  the current revision, which the tool cannot confirm.
- Piles missing position, levels or diameter are listed as undrawable with the
  blocker named, rather than placed at the origin with a guessed size.

## Cost

More verbose than plain numbers, and every UI component has to render a state.
Accepted — see [[Reduced levels and datums]] for the failure mode this prevents.

## Related

- [[Socket compliance is indeterminate by default]]

# Reference library

A catalogue of the geotechnical reference material held locally, so it can be
found from the notes that use it.

**These are pointers, not copies.** The standards, papers and textbooks are
licensed or copyright material and are not reproduced in this vault — the notes
record what a document covers and where it sits, and the document itself stays
where it is. Anything relied on for a job is read from the source.

Local root: `C:\Users\pored\Downloads\G materials`

## By topic

- [[Library - Australian Standards]] — AS series held locally
- [[Library - RMS and TfNSW specifications]] — roads specs and test methods
- [[Library - Pells papers on Sydney sandstone and shale]] — the local rock-socket literature
- [[Library - plate load testing]] — PLT procedure, spreadsheets and training
- [[Library - salinity and sodic soils]] — western Sydney salinity guidance
- [[Library - reference texts and parameter sources]] — textbooks and correlation sources

## Housekeeping notes

The root folder holds several duplicates — `AS 1726 2017` and `AS1726-2017`
are both present, `AS3798` appears twice, and `Australian and RMS Standards/`
contains a second copy of the whole `Australian/` and `RMS/` trees. Two files
are zero bytes (`CG24-0518-A Rev 1.pdf`, `CG25-0768-1, Site plan_BB.pdf`) and
will not open. Worth a tidy before this becomes the reference of record.

notes.title: Library - Pells papers on Sydney sandstone and shale
notes.body:
# Library - Pells papers on Sydney sandstone and shale

`G materials/Pells Paper/`. The local literature behind how sockets in Sydney
sandstone and shale are classified and designed — directly relevant to
[[Rock socket length]] and [[Weathered siltstone]].

| Paper | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| Pells, Mostyn & Wong (2019) — Classification of sandstones and shales in the Sydney region | The classification scheme used locally to describe Sydney basin rock |
| Pells — The design of socketed piles in rock | Socket design method, side resistance and end bearing |
| Pells — Bored piles socketed into shale and sandstone | Field behaviour of sockets in the local materials |
| Pells — Foundations on sandstone and shale in the Sydney region | Founding practice across the basin |
| Substance and mass properties for the design of engineering structures in the Hawkesbury Sandstone | Intact vs mass properties — the distinction that matters for defect-controlled rock |

## What to take from these

Intact strength and mass behaviour diverge in bedded rock, which is the point
made in [[Rock strength classes]]. A socket in shale that rates medium on hand
specimens can be governed by bedding partings rather than intact strength.

> Copyright papers. Cite them, do not paste them.

# Library - plate load testing

`G materials/Plate Load Testing/`. Procedure, computation spreadsheets and
training for the light and dynamic plate load kit.

| File | What it is |

| `050-Setup Proceedure for PLT Draft 4 Feb 2024.docx/.pdf` | Our setup procedure — draft status, check before relying on it |

| `PLT Calculations for AX01a.pdf`, `Calculations.pdf` | Worked computation |

| `BedAnlAx01a_engl V40a.pdf` | Equipment manual |

## Caution

The Ev2/Evd relationship is a correlation, not an identity, and it is
material-dependent. Reporting a dynamic result as if it were a static modulus
without stating the correlation is the same class of error described in
[[DCP testing]].

notes.title: Library - reference texts and parameter sources
notes.body:
# Library - reference texts and parameter sources

Where a parameter comes from when it is not measured on the job. Every value
taken from here is a published correlation, not a site measurement, and is
recorded as such — see [[Why pile data carries provenance]].

| Source | Use |
|---|---|
| Look, *Handbook of Geotechnical Investigation and Design Tables* (2014) | First stop for indicative parameters and correlations |
| `Correlations of Soil Properties.pdf` | Correlation compendium |
| `8 Determination of Geotechnical Parameters.pdf` | Parameter selection method |
| Schnaid, *In Situ Testing in Geomechanics* | Interpreting in-situ tests |
| Das, *Principles of Geotechnical Engineering* (8th ed.) | General reference |
| Lambe & Whitman, *Soil Mechanics* | Fundamentals |
| `SPT direct methods for prediction of pile bearing capacity...pdf` | SPT-to-pile-capacity methods |
| `Munsell Color Chart.pdf` | Colour description — pair with [[Soil description order]] |
| `Shallow Bearing Capacity - Various Methods and Settlement Rev 4.xltm` | Our bearing capacity spreadsheet |
| `Earth pressure calculations.xlsx` | Retaining wall pressures |
| `Working Platforms for tracked plant.pdf` | Working platform design for piling rigs |

## The discipline that matters here

A correlation is valid for the material and test it was derived from. Carrying
an SPT-based capacity into a rock socket, or a sand correlation into clay,
produces a confident number with no basis. State the source and the assumed
material whenever one of these is used.

## Related

- [[DCP testing]]
- [[Library - plate load testing]]

notes.title: Rock strength classes
notes.body:
# Rock strength classes

Field estimates of unconfined compressive strength, per
[[AS 1726 soil and rock description]]. Assessed with a geological pick and
hand pressure, and recorded as an estimate — a field class is not a laboratory
UCS result and should never be reported as one.

| Class | Approx. UCS | Field behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| EL — extremely low | < 0.6 MPa | Crumbles under firm hand pressure |
| VL — very low | 0.6–2 MPa | Peels with a knife; deep pick indentation |
| L — low | 2–6 MPa | Pick indents; cannot be peeled |
| M — medium | 6–20 MPa | Shallow pick indentation |
| H — high | 20–60 MPa | Hand specimen breaks with one firm hammer blow |
| VH — very high | 60–200 MPa | Several blows to break |
| EH — extremely high | > 200 MPa | Chips only |

## The judgement to be careful with

Strength varies with moisture and with defect spacing. A tightly bedded siltstone
can rate medium on intact fragments and behave far weaker as a mass because it
parts along bedding. Log the defects as well as the intact strength.

## Related

- [[Rock weathering classes]]
- [[Rock socket length]]

notes.title: Rock weathering classes
notes.body:
# Rock weathering classes

Per [[AS 1726 soil and rock description]], in decreasing order of weathering:

- **RS** — residual soil. Soil texture; original fabric destroyed.
- **XW** — extremely weathered. Has soil strength but rock fabric survives.
- **HW** — highly weathered. Discoloured throughout, strength much reduced.
- **MW** — moderately weathered. Discoloured, partly reduced strength.
- **SW** — slightly weathered. Slight discolouration, strength near fresh.
- **FR** — fresh. No visible weathering.

## Where the founding decision sits

For bored piers, the usual requirement is founding in rock that is at worst
moderately weathered and of a stated minimum strength — weathering class alone
does not carry the requirement. XW material can look convincingly like rock in
the base of a pier and still behave as a stiff soil. Class it honestly and pair
it with a strength assessment; see [[Rock strength classes]].

## Related

- [[Weathered siltstone]]
- [[Bored pier inspection]]
notes.text: Rock weathering classes Per AS 1726 soil and rock description, in decreasing order of weathering: RS — residual soil. Soil texture; original fabric destroyed. XW — extremely weathered. Has soil strength but rock fabric survives. HW — highly weathered. Discoloured throughout, strength much reduced. MW — moderately weathered. Discoloured, partly reduced strength. SW — slightly weathered. Slight discolouration, strength near fresh. FR — fresh. No visible weathering. Where the founding decision sits For bored piers, the usual requirement is founding in rock that is at worst moderately weathered and of a stated minimum strength — weathering class alone does not carry the requirement. XW material can look convincingly like rock in the base of a pier and still behave as a stiff soil. Class it honestly and pair it with a strength assessment; see Rock strength classes. Related Weathered siltstone Bored pier inspection

notes.title: Soil description order
notes.body:
# Soil description order

The sequence a soil description is written in, per [[AS 1726 soil and rock description]].

**SOIL NAME: plasticity or particle characteristics, colour, secondary
components, structure, consistency or density, moisture, origin**

Example as logged: `CLAY: high plasticity, pale grey mottled red-orange, trace
fine sand, stiff, moist, residual`

## Why the order is fixed

Logs are read as a column, scanned for change. Putting the governing material
first means the eye catches the boundary. Everything after it is qualification.

## Consistency vs density

Consistency terms (very soft, soft, firm, stiff, very stiff, hard) are for
cohesive soils. Density index terms (very loose, loose, medium dense, dense,
very dense) are for granular soils. Mixing the two — "dense clay" — is a logging
error that will be picked up in review.

## Related

- [[Rock weathering classes]]
- [[Borehole log conventions]]

notes.title: Weathered siltstone
notes.body:
# Weathered siltstone

The material most of our western Sydney bored piers found on. Ashfield Shale and
related Wianamatta Group siltstones, weathered from the surface down.

## Typical profile

Residual high-plasticity silty clay, pale grey mottled red-orange, roughly
0.0–1.2 m thick, over extremely to moderately weathered siltstone. Rockhead is
often gradational rather than a clean surface, which is why proving it needs the
pier base inspected rather than a depth called from a nearby borehole.

*Source: STS report 26/0988, 24-26 Carter Street Lidcombe, 18 piers inspected
27 Jul 2026 — piers founded 1.8–3.3 m below platform with sockets 0.6–2.0 m.*

## What to watch

- Slaking. Exposed siltstone softens quickly once wet, which is the reason
  [[AS 2159 piling]] wants concrete placed promptly.
- The XW/HW boundary is where most disagreements happen. See
  [[Rock weathering classes]].

## Related

- [[Bored pier inspection]]

notes.title: Bored pier inspection
notes.body:
# Bored pier inspection

What gets checked and recorded at the base of a bored pier before concrete.

## On site

1. Confirm the pier reference against the [[Borehole log conventions|structural drawing]] — pier tag, not just position.
2. Record depth to founding level and depth to rockhead, both below the working platform.
3. Describe the founding material: [[Rock weathering classes|weathering]], [[Rock strength classes|strength]], defects.
4. Measure the achieved socket — see [[Rock socket length]].
5. Confirm the base is clean and free of loose or softened material.
6. Note groundwater — see [[Groundwater observations]].
7. Photograph the base with the pier tag visible in frame.

## What the report can and cannot say

It can say the exposed material was competent and consistent with the design
assumption at the time of inspection. It cannot certify the pile. Acceptance
against the design requirement needs the required socket length from the
approved drawing, which the inspection report often does not carry — see
[[Socket compliance is indeterminate by default]].

## The recurring failure

Reporting a depth without the platform level it was measured from. A depth below
ground is not a level, and once the platform is cut or filled the number means
nothing. See [[Reduced levels and datums]].

## Related

- [[AS 2159 piling]]

notes.title: Borehole log conventions
notes.body:
# Borehole log conventions

How our logs are laid out, and the reasons behind the layout.

## Columns

Depth scale, graphic log, material description, sampling and in-situ tests,
water, and remarks. The depth scale runs downward with the description beside
it, so a reader scanning for a boundary tracks one column.

## Description

Per [[Soil description order]] for soil and the weathering plus strength pairing
for rock — [[Rock weathering classes]], [[Rock strength classes]].

## What must appear on every log

- Hole reference, and the method and rig used.
- Surface RL and its datum, or an explicit note that it is assumed. See
  [[Reduced levels and datums]].
- Date drilled and who logged it.
- Groundwater observations with timing — [[Groundwater observations]].
- Where the log was terminated and why: target depth, refusal, or obstruction.

## Related

- [[AS 1726 soil and rock description]]

notes.title: DCP testing
notes.body:
# DCP testing

Dynamic cone penetrometer — 9 kg hammer, 510 mm drop, driving a 20 mm cone.
Blows per 100 mm increment. Quick, cheap, and shallow.

## What it is good for

Consistency and density profiling in the top couple of metres, checking that
founding material is as expected across a footprint, and identifying soft spots
and fill.

## What it is not

It is not a bearing capacity test. Correlations from blow counts to allowable
bearing pressure carry wide scatter, and they are correlations for the material
type assumed. Applying a sand correlation to clay produces a confident number
that is wrong.

## Reporting

Report the blow count profile. If an allowable bearing pressure is given,
state the correlation used, the assumed material and the depth range it applies
over, and flag refusal or possible obstruction rather than reading it as very
dense material.

## Related

- [[AS 2870 residential site classification]]
- [[Groundwater observations]]

notes.title: Graph engineering
notes.body:
# Graph engineering

A way of laying out agent work as a dependency map rather than a list of steps.

- **Node** — one unit of work. One input, one output. The smaller and more
  defined, the more useful.
- **Edge** — a real dependency. It exists only when the second node consumes
  what the first produced.

## The fake-edge test

Write the steps as boxes, draw an arrow between each consecutive pair, then ask
of every arrow: *does data from A actually go into B?* If not, the arrow is an
artefact of the order you typed things in, and the wait it imposes is free time
you are giving away. Anything with no incoming arrow can start immediately.

Most workflows hold two or three fake edges. "Review file A, then review file B"
is the classic — B never reads A's output.

## The diamond

One node fans out to several independent nodes, which all converge on one node
that combines them. The convergence waits for the slowest branch rather than the
sum of all branches.

Two conditions. The parallel nodes must be genuinely independent, and the
convergence must actually need all of them. If it only needs one, the rest are
wasted work.

## Checker nodes

Parallelism removes the natural checkpoints where you would have spotted a bad
result. A branch that returns nothing, or hallucinates, feeds into synthesis
alongside good branches and the final answer is confidently wrong — with the
error diluted enough to be hard to trace.

A checker sits between the parallel layer and the convergence and does no work
of its own. It looks for empty outputs, outputs that contradict each other,
off-topic results, low confidence, and format errors that would break parsing.
Flagged branches are retried or dropped, never merged.

## Static vs dynamic

Static graphs are fixed before the run: fast, predictable, auditable. Dynamic
graphs grow as they run, with nodes deciding what comes next — flexible, but
what actually ran is not what you drew, which makes debugging and auditing
harder. Reach for static first. Never use dynamic where you need to audit
exactly what ran and why, which for engineering work is most of the time.

## Where this already exists in our work

The `geoflow-verify-graph` skill in this repo is a diamond: independent
read-only verifier agents fan out, a barrier collects their reports, findings
are reduced, fixed, and re-verified. The reduce step is the checker.

## Caution for engineering use

The parallel-then-combine shape is right for review and search. It is wrong for
anything where one branch's finding should change what another branch looks for
— which happens often in ground investigation, where a single unexpected result
should redirect the whole enquiry rather than being averaged in with the rest.

## Related

- [[Reverse prompting]]
- [[Socket compliance is indeterminate by default]] — a checker in a different guise

notes.title: Groundwater observations
notes.body:
# Groundwater observations

A water level in an open hole is an observation at a moment, not a water table.

## What to record

- Depth to water, and the time since the hole was advanced to that depth.
- Whether water was added during drilling.
- Whether the level was still rising when observed.
- Seepage: at what depth, and whether it was a defined horizon.
- "Not encountered" as an explicit statement, because absence of a note is not
  the same as absence of water.

## Why the caveat matters

In low-permeability clay a hole can take days to equilibrate, so a short-term
reading understates the standing level. In fractured rock the reading may reflect
one defect rather than a regional level. Neither is a design groundwater level
without a standpipe and repeat readings.

## Related

- [[Bored pier inspection]]
- [[DCP testing]]

notes.title: Reduced levels and datums
notes.body:
# Reduced levels and datums

RL is height above a datum, increasing upward. Depth is measured downward from a
surface. They are not interchangeable and the confusion between them causes real
errors.

```
depth below platform = platform RL − toe RL
toe RL              = platform RL − depth below platform
```

## Rules we hold to

- Every depth is recorded with the surface it was measured from.
- Every level records its datum — AHD, or a stated site datum, or "assumed".
- An assumed datum is written as assumed. A level on an assumed datum cannot be
  compared with a surveyed one, and a model built on it is dimensionally right
  and absolutely wrong.

## Where it bites

A report that tabulates depths below ground with no platform RL cannot be turned
into a model with true levels. The pile viewer marks the platform level
`inferred` in that case and flags every level derived from it, rather than
quietly assuming zero — see [[Why pile data carries provenance]].

## Related

- [[Borehole log conventions]]

notes.title: Reverse prompting
notes.body:
# Reverse prompting

Instead of writing a prompt, hand over context and let the agent ask what else it
needs. The useful form is a single question:

> Based on what you know about me and my goals, what more could I give you so you
> can help faster and take more off my plate?

Then: *what can you do right now that moves us toward that?*

## Why it works

Not because the model knows things you don't. It works because the model can see
the shape of the gap in what you've given it, and asking forces you to articulate
things you'd otherwise leave tacit. Most bad AI output traces to missing context
rather than weak reasoning, and this closes that gap faster than you guessing what
to include.

## Where it does not

The model cannot ask about a domain it has no purchase on, so in narrow technical
work you still have to seed it. And questions cost your attention — a long
interview that produces a note you could have written in two minutes is a net
loss. Keep interviews short and aimed at knowledge that is genuinely in your head
and nowhere else.

## How it is used here

The Capture mode in the [[Index|second brain]] viewer is this idea made concrete:
pick a note type and it interviews you, then emits a vault-ready Markdown note
with frontmatter, tags and wikilinks. The questions are a fixed bank rather than
an LLM, so it works offline and produces the same structure every time. A live
model asking follow-ups would need an API key and a backend, which the static
worker does not have.

## Related

- [[Template - site inspection note]]

notes.title: Rock socket length
notes.body:
# Rock socket length

The length of pier penetrating competent rock, measured from proved rockhead to
the toe.

```
socket = top-of-bedrock RL − toe RL
```

## Required vs achieved

Two different numbers that get confused constantly.

- **Required** comes from the approved structural drawing or pile schedule. It
  is a design requirement.
- **Achieved** is what was built and measured on site.

A report giving only the achieved socket cannot demonstrate compliance. The tool
handles this by refusing to call it a pass — see
[[Socket compliance is indeterminate by default]].

## Measuring honestly

Rockhead is often gradational in [[Weathered siltstone]], so the socket depends
on where you call the top of competent rock. Record the weathering class at that
level, not just the depth, so the call can be reviewed.

## Related

- [[Bored pier inspection]]
- [[Why pile data carries provenance]]

notes.title: AS 1726 soil and rock description
notes.body:
# AS 1726 soil and rock description

AS 1726:2017 *Geotechnical site investigations* is the Australian standard that
sets out how ground is described and logged. It is the reason two engineers
logging the same core should produce comparable descriptions.

> The standard itself is copyright and is not reproduced here. Clause numbers
> are recorded so the passage can be found; check the actual document before
> relying on any of this on a job.

## What it governs

- The vocabulary for soil and rock description, and the order terms appear in —
  see [[Soil description order]].
- Weathering and strength classification for rock — see
  [[Rock weathering classes]] and [[Rock strength classes]].
- Sampling and in-situ test reporting requirements.
- What a borehole log must show — see [[Borehole log conventions]].

## Why the order matters

The description order is not stylistic. A log is read by people scanning a
column for a change in material, so the governing term comes first and the
qualifiers follow. Writing "brown clay, high plasticity" instead of
"CLAY: high plasticity, brown" breaks the scan.

## Related

- [[AS 2159 piling]] — founding requirements that rely on these descriptions
- [[Weathered siltstone]] — the description applied on most of our Sydney work

notes.title: AS 2159 piling
notes.body:
# AS 2159 piling

AS 2159:2009 *Piling — Design and installation* governs pile design and
construction, including bored piers.

> Summarised, not reproduced. Clause references are pointers, not quotations.

## What we lean on it for

- **Base cleanliness and concrete placement.** Clause 7.6.5(c) is the one cited
  in most of our inspection reports: loose or softened material at the base is
  removed before concrete, and concrete follows promptly after drilling,
  cleaning and geotechnical approval. See [[Bored pier inspection]].
- **Founding verification.** The pier is proved into the material the design
  assumed, not merely to a nominated depth.
- **Risk rating and the geotechnical strength reduction factor.** The standard
  ties the factor to how much site investigation and construction control there
  actually is — better investigation earns a higher factor.

## The practical consequence for inspections

Our sign-off is that the exposed founding material was competent and consistent
with the design assumption at the time of inspection. That is a narrower claim
than "the pile is adequate", and the report wording keeps it narrow. Acceptance
of the pile as a structural element remains with the design engineer — see
[[Socket compliance is indeterminate by default]].

## Related

- [[Rock socket length]]
- [[AS 1726 soil and rock description]]

notes.title: AS 2870 residential site classification
notes.body:
# AS 2870 residential site classification

AS 2870 *Residential slabs and footings* classifies sites by how much the soil
moves with moisture change, which then drives the footing design.

> Summarised. Class definitions and design tables live in the standard.

## Classes in short

- **A** — stable, little or no ground movement from moisture change (sand, rock)
- **S** — slightly reactive clay
- **M** — moderately reactive clay or silt
- **H1 / H2** — highly reactive clay
- **E** — extremely reactive clay
- **P** — problem site: fill, soft soil, mine subsidence, landslip, or where the
  above cannot be applied

## What decides the class

Characteristic surface movement `y_s`, calculated from soil reactivity and the
depth of the design suction change. Reactivity comes from shrink-swell index
testing, not from the description alone — a clay that looks the same in two
suburbs can classify differently.

## The trap

Fill, cut, and trees change the answer. A site with uncontrolled fill is P
regardless of the clay underneath it, and removing a large tree can leave years
of ongoing heave. Classification without checking site history is guesswork.

## Related

- [[Soil description order]]
- [[DCP testing]]
